Plus, tech stocks set to rebound

Stranger Things

 

If you had shown up in Hollywood pitching a script about Netflix’s recent struggles, it wouldn’t have gotten past the executive assistant to the executive producer. The plot has too many holes. 

 

Its shares began slumping last September amid talk the company would buy the studio and streaming assets of Warner Bros. By February, when it looked like Netflix had won a bidding war, it had shed nearly $200 billion in market value.

 

Shareholders celebrated when management decided to walk away following Skydance’s winning counteroffer, pocketing a $2.8 billion break fee. But only briefly—the stock has kept sliding, hitting a two-year low this month.

 

Netflix’s third-quarter results are due Tuesday afternoon and the stock has dropped after each of its last five reports. There are concerns about subscriber churn and the recent sacking of its content boss amid a round of layoffs.

 

Its slide can’t be explained by a creative soft patch. The company has lost as much market value in a year as Walt Disney’s entire market capitalization all while earnings expectations for this year have been stable.

 

So maybe a competitive threat from the new media giant on the block is making investors nervous?

 

Skydance is formidable now, combining two streaming rivals, a major studio and a rich content library. But it also faces management tumult and carries a daunting amount of debt with an even higher interest bill than anticipated. If a rival has to pinch pennies, it can be a boon to market leader Netflix when shopping for hit shows.

 

Industry scuttlebutt from alternative data provider Heron Intelligence points to a different competitor: YouTube.

 

The Alphabet subsidiary is gaining eyeballs through creator content that Netflix is struggling to match. One executive interviewed points out that Netflix’s “mode of discovery is so fundamentally different from YouTube’s.”

 

Competitive threats are growing amid “streamflation” concerns—financially pinched households cutting or pausing subscriptions to services such as Netflix. It isn’t just YouTube. Rivals such as Tubi, Pluto TV and Roku, that offer free, ad-supported shows and movies, also benefit from consumer angst.

 

But Netflix is pushing ahead with a hybrid model, targeting about $3 billion in ad revenue this year—around 6% of its total revenue. Analysts at Morgan Stanley think that can grow by more than half next year.

 

It would make a big difference financially. Weak subscriber growth in the third quarter would be taken poorly, but investors might be underestimating how much ads can offset it.

 

And Netflix management dodged a bullet by wisely not paying $83 billion, including debt, for Warner Bros. It’s been scooping up its own shares instead—some $27 billion from 2023 through this June, hitting a record pace during the second quarter as it put Skydance’s breakup fee to work. 

 

Netflix’s bang for the buyback buck is rising too: Its free cash flow yield just hit a 15-year high.

 

That isn’t the sort of story that draws you in immediately. Try sticking with it.
